newsitem.title: USA: Judge dismisses California suits against gun maker.
newsitem.headline: Judge dismisses California suits against gun maker.

text.p: A judge on Tuesday dismissed lawsuits against the maker of semi-automatic assault weapons used by a gunman who killed eight people during a 1993 rampage in a San Francisco office building.

In a victory for the gun industry, San Francisco Superior Court Judge James Warren granted summary judgment to gun maker Navegar Inc. of Miami, dismissing wrongful death lawsuits filed by relatives of the victims.
Attorneys for the victims said they were disappointed by the ruling and planned to appeal.

The case stems from a July 1, 1993, shooting at a San Francisco office building when gunman Gian Luigi Ferri, 55, went on a shooting rampage at a law firm, killing eight people and wounding six before taking his own life.

In 1994, families of seven of the victims sued Navegar, which makes the TEC-DC9 semi-automatic pistols used by Ferri in the 101 California Street shooting. Ferri bought two TEC-DC9s in Nevada, where their sale was legal, and brought them to California.
Victims filed separate lawsuits against the gun manufacturer, but Judge Warren consolidated the complaints to speed up trial. His ruling on Tuesday dismissed all of the suits against Navegar.
Lawyers for the victims' families argued that the gun manufacturer should be held liable because its products were designed, distributed and marketed for mass killing.
Navegar sought to have the suits dismissed, pointing out that no court in California has ever held a gun manufacturer responsible for criminal shootings.
The case was the first of its kind in the nation brought by shooting victims against an assault weapons manufacturer, attorneys said.
The American Shooting Sports Council, which represents firearm and ammunition manufacturers, praised the ruling as "sound and rational."
Attorneys for families of the victims said they were confident their argument would sway the appeals court.

"We believe that .... the courts will find that a gun manufacturer that sells a gun designed for mass destruction should be held accountable when the gun is used for that purpose," said Dennis Henigan, legal director for the Centre to Prevent Handgun Violence, which represented the plaintiffs.
Several of the victims' families have also sued building security and the building management company at the 101 California offices. Those claims were not affected by Tuesday's ruling.
